The Mother of God: Milk Giver

Icons

Theotokos

The Mother of God: Milk Giver

Galaktotrophousa · Mlekopitatelnitsa · Typikonissa

What is depictedHistory and traditionPublished explanationSources

Scripture

John 1:14

King James Version · Scripture previews

The OCA’s Milk-Giver account follows a venerated image from the Lavra of Saint Savva near Jerusalem to Saint Savva of Serbia and the Athonite cell at Karyes connected with Hilandar. The source prints January 12 as its commemoration.

[1] Heading; entire three-paragraph account

What is depicted

The type depicts Mary nursing the infant Christ. The Uffizi’s collection entry identifies the nursing Mother of God as Milk-Giver; this title describes the composition rather than establishing that every image of it is the particular icon preserved at Karyes.

[2] Artwork description

History and tradition

According to the tradition published by the OCA, Saint Savva the Sanctified foretold that a royal pilgrim with his own name would visit the Lavra and should receive the icon. When Saint Savva of Serbia visited in the thirteenth century, the founder’s staff fell at his feet. The monks gave him the staff, the Milk-Giver, and the Three Hands image. He took the icon to Athos and placed it to the right of the iconostasis in the Karyes cell church.

[1] First three paragraphs

Published explanation

The OCA explains the additional title Typikonissa by the preservation of Saint Savva’s Rule, or Typikon, at the cell. John’s statement about the Word becoming flesh is presented below as Scripture, in the identified KJV edition.

[1] Final sentence

And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

[3] John 1:14
